title: Gurdwara Bangla Sahib Opened Its Doors as Delhi Police Turned on Student Protesters
excerpt: As tear gas and lathi charges dispersed thousands during the Chalo Sansad march on July 20, the historic Sikh shrine near Jantar Mantar became a refuge for injured and fleeing demonstrators.
body:
When Delhi Police unleashed tear gas and lathi charges on thousands of student protesters attempting to march toward Parliament on July 20, many found themselves with nowhere to run. Metro stations had been shuttered. Internet service was cut. Barricades blocked every exit. But a few hundred metres from the chaos, the golden dome of Gurdwara Bangla Sahib offered what the state would not: sanctuary.

A Refuge Amid the Crackdown

The historic gurdwara on Baba Kharak Singh Marg became a shelter for students and protesters fleeing batons and tear gas during the Chalo Sansad march. As security forces dispersed the crowd of over one lakh on the first day of Parliament's monsoon session, injured demonstrators streamed into the shrine seeking first aid, food, and a safe place to regroup.

CNN reported that about 150 protesters were taken to hospital with injuries. Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital alone recorded 65 medico-legal cases by 7 pm that day. Delhi Police said 118 of its officers were also hurt.

Eyewitnesses described authorities beating demonstrators, dragging students along streets, detaining them in police buses, and deploying what protesters said were electrified barricades. The Delhi Metro Rail Corporation had closed five stations, including the major Rajiv Chowk interchange, leaving many trapped in the area with few options for escape.

"Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital alone recorded 65 medico-legal cases by 7 pm that day."

The Sikh Tradition of Langar and Seva

Gurdwara Bangla Sahib, one of Delhi's most prominent Sikh shrines, is known for its massive community kitchen that feeds an estimated 10,000 visitors daily. The practice of langar — serving free meals to all comers regardless of religion, caste, or background — is a cornerstone of Sikh faith, rooted in the principle of seva, or selfless service.

The Delhi Sikh Gurdwara Management Committee (DSGMC) has a documented history of supporting protesters at Jantar Mantar. During earlier protests by Tamil Nadu farmers, the committee delivered langar food twice daily to the demonstration site and adjusted the menu when volunteers learned the southern farmers preferred rice to chapatis.

Livemint reported on the Sikh community's role in providing food, first aid, and refuge to the student demonstrators, with the phrase "look for men in turbans" circulating as a message of solidarity among protesters at the site.

"Delhi Police said 118 of its officers were also hurt.</p> <blockquote class="pull-quote"><p>"But just in a flash, I don't know what happened, the police started hitting us with batons."

A Movement That Has Outgrown Its Origins

The Cockroach Janta Party's protests, which began on June 6, have grown into the largest demonstrations against the Modi government in years. Climate activist Sonam Wangchuk's hunger strike at the site, and his forcible removal by police on July 18, galvanized support. On July 20, CJP representatives met Union Health Minister J.P. Nadda to present demands including Wangchuk's release, Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation, and ₹1 crore compensation for families of NEET aspirants who died by suicide.

The gurdwara's response fits a broader pattern of solidarity sustaining the protest into its seventh week — from strangers arriving with home-cooked meals to volunteers serving tea each morning. For the Indian diaspora, the images carry particular weight. Sikh gurdwaras from California to London to Melbourne have long served as community anchors during crises. The sight of a centuries-old Delhi shrine sheltering tear-gassed Gen Z protesters connects that global tradition to a deeply domestic reckoning.
